header.title: Questions people ask first
header.sub: Short answers, each with a link to the chapter that has the long one.

questions.q: Do I need to run the platform?
questions.a: No. We host the ladder. You need a GitHub account, an ONNX model and a manifest, and the game’s starter kit lets you play the same match on your own machine with nothing at stake.

questions.q: Can I use PyTorch, JAX, or anything else?
questions.a: Yes. You submit one self-contained model.onnx, built however you like. We trained the platform’s baselines in PyTorch, exported them through torch.onnx and rewrote them to float16 initializers.

ONNX opsets 13 to 19 and an allowlist: Conv, MatMul, Gemm, the usual activations and reductions, Resize, Gather, Slice and the rest the format chapter lists. The list covers operators and leaves attributes alone, so a dilated Conv passes. ConvTranspose is off the list; upsample with Resize.

more.label: The list, in the format chapter

questions.q: How is size measured, and which class am I in?
questions.a: Size is the bytes of model.onnx plus the bytes of manifest.json, on files the platform re-hashes. We compress and estimate nothing, so no way of packing your weights can understate it. Admission gives you the smallest class whose cap fits; each season sets its caps, and the home page shows them. Float16 initializers halve the file, so you fit about twice the parameters you would in float32.

No. A class limits size and nothing else. The turn deadline bounds compute: input adaptation, inference and output adaptation share it, and the platform divides one turn’s deadline among the seats it plays together. A graph too slow for its share misses the turn and takes a strike. Admission reports your inference time and accepts you whatever it is.

One JSON object per turn: the board size, your living ants, the enemy ants, food and hills in view, and the water found so far as a run-length mask. It gets no score, no turn number and no memory between turns. Owners are relative to you, so each seat of a match sees the same encoding.
One of N, E, S, W or - for each of your ants, in the order the observation lists them. You may hold every ant still; a missing answer costs a strike.

questions.q: What is the manifest, and why is it not code?
questions.a: It declares the name, dtype and shape of what your graph takes and returns, and carries one adapter expression per input: a small JSON program that turns the observation into that tensor. It is data so the evaluator can count its operations under a budget, and so we can weigh it into your size beside the weights. You do not write the output side: the referee reads your policy head, because the channel order is a rule of the game. The baselines generate their manifest from the code that trains them, and a test proves the two encodings agree.

more.label: A real manifest, piece by piece

questions.q: Can I enter more than one model?
questions.a: Yes. A model starts as a name, and you may hold as many as the season allows. Each is its own entry with its own rating, and one of yours may beat another like any opponent. Each model has one version in admission at a time, and a season may cap how many of yours are in flight together.

questions.q: Can I resubmit the same weights?
questions.a: Not in one season. A season counts one entry per set of weights, so the same file cannot take a second place on the ladder. Each attempt is a new version, and an edit to the manifest’s formatting alone changes its hash and its size.

You upload the two files to the one-shot URLs the submission answers with. We re-hash them against what you declared, measure the model into a class and play one trial match against a baseline, which passes if it finishes under the strike limit, win or lose. The version then goes active and plays without a break, and the model’s previous version keeps playing until the new one is through.

questions.q: How do I test before submitting?
questions.a: tinybrains check measures what admission measures, over the game’s reference observations, with the same expression engine for the manifest and the same runtime for the graph. tinybrains adapt writes the tensors your adapters build, so you can compare them with your trainer’s encoder. The starter kit’s match files play your model against a baseline through the real engine. A local pass does not guarantee admission, and admission alone decides your class.

Each match counts on Open, and a match between versions of one class counts on that class’s ladder too. We show μ − 3σ, so a rating rises as it settles; a half-filled circle marks one still settling, and those appear on the ladder too.
